The Analects. A collection of sayings and conversations attributed to Confucius and his disciples, compiled in China around the fifth century BCE. It stands as the foundational text of Confucianism, shaping Chinese philosophy and governance for millennia.

The text was written as brief aphorisms and dialogues, emphasizing virtue, propriety, and proper relationships. Confucius himself lived from 551 to 479 BCE during the Spring and Autumn period of China, but he did not write the text himself. The name Lunyu, meaning classified sayings or collected conversations in Classical Chinese, reflects this form.

The core themes include li, propriety and ritual; ren, humaneness; and self-cultivation through learning and moral discipline. The Analects heavily influenced Chinese education for over two thousand years, serving as the primary textbook for civil service exams. Han Dynasty editors organized it into twenty books not chronologically but by topic and context.

One famous passage captures its spirit: the Master said, when you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it—this is knowledge. The text stands at the centre of a web of Chinese thought, contrasting with the Tao Te Ching's Taoist alternative philosophy and later interacting with Buddhist thought in East Asia.
